paths.title: Rust Foundations
paths.summary: The first steps of Rust: a program that runs, values you can change, functions that hand work back to you, and the ownership rule that makes Rust different.
paths.subject: Programming

lessons.title: Your first Rust program
lessons.summary: Where execution starts, what a statement is, and why println! has an exclamation mark.
objectives: Name the function a Rust binary starts in.
Explain what a statement does and where one ends.
Recognise a macro call and say how it differs from a function call.

sections.heading: A program starts at main
sections.body: Every Rust binary begins at a function called main. When the program runs, Rust calls main and executes the statements inside it from top to bottom. Nothing outside main runs on its own.

sections.heading: What happens when this program runs
steps: Rust starts the program and calls main.
The single statement inside main runs and prints the text.
main returns, and the program ends.

sections.body: println! is a macro, which is why it ends with an exclamation mark. A macro can work with your source in ways an ordinary function cannot, such as inserting values into the text it prints.
A common mistake is to write println("Hello, world!") without the exclamation mark. Rust then looks for an ordinary function named println, which does not exist, and the program does not compile.

checks.prompt: Which function does a Rust binary start in?
checks.explanation: Rust calls main first. The other names have no special meaning to the language.

checks.prompt: What does the semicolon at the end of println!("Hello, world!"); do?
options: It marks the end of the statement
It is optional and changes nothing
checks.explanation: In Rust a semicolon ends a statement. Leaving it out where a statement is expected is a compile error.

checks.prompt: The exclamation mark in println! is what marks it as a macro call.
checks.explanation: Macro calls end with an exclamation mark; a plain name followed by parentheses calls a function.

lessons.title: Storing values in variables
lessons.summary: Bindings, immutability by default, and how Rust works out a type for you.
objectives: Create a binding with let and make it changeable with mut.
Say why reassigning an immutable binding fails to compile.
Explain how Rust infers the type of a number.

sections.heading: Bindings are immutable until you say otherwise
sections.body: A let binding gives a name to a value: let score = 10; That binding is immutable by default, so writing score = 11; afterwards is a compile error. Adding mut allows the value to change: let mut score = 10;

sections.heading: A binding that changes
Three ways to name a value
rows: A fixed binding: it cannot be reassigned.
A changeable binding: it can be reassigned while it is in scope.
A constant: always written with a type and fixed at compile time.

sections.heading: Types are usually inferred
sections.body: Nothing above names a type. Rust sees 10 used as a whole number and infers i32, its default integer type. Text written between double quotes is borrowed text, written &str. You can always write the type yourself when it helps the reader.

checks.prompt: Which binding can be given a new value later?
checks.explanation: Only mut allows reassignment. const and a plain let are fixed once created.

checks.prompt: Given let count = 3; which line fails to compile?
checks.explanation: count was created without mut, so it cannot be assigned a new value.

checks.prompt: With let score = 10; Rust still works out a type for score even though none was written.
checks.explanation: Type inference fills in the type from how the value is used, so score becomes an i32 by default.

lessons.title: Functions that return values
lessons.summary: Parameters with types, a declared return type, and the final expression that produces the answer.
objectives: Read a function signature and say what it returns.
Explain why the final expression has no semicolon.
Trace a function call from the caller to its result.

sections.heading: A return type is part of the promise
sections.body: A function declares what it gives back: fn add(a: i32, b: i32) -> i32 The arrow is followed by the return type. Each parameter needs its type written out, because Rust does not guess across function boundaries.

sections.heading: The last expression is the result
Following the call to add(2, 3)
steps: add binds those values to its parameters a and b.
The final expression a + b is evaluated and becomes the value of the call.
main stores that value in total and prints it.

sections.body: The body of add ends with a + b and no semicolon. Without the semicolon it is an expression whose value becomes the return value. Adding one turns it into a statement that produces nothing, which no longer matches the declared i32.
If add ended with a + b; the function would return () instead of i32, and the compiler would reject it. The semicolon throws the value away.

checks.prompt: In fn add(a: i32, b: i32) -> i32, what does -> i32 declare?
options: The type of the first parameter
The type of the value the function returns
The number of arguments the function takes
checks.explanation: The arrow introduces the return type, so add gives back an i32.

checks.prompt: Why does a + b have no semicolon in fn add?
options: Semicolons are not allowed inside functions
It must stay the final expression so its value is returned
It prints the result to the terminal
checks.explanation: The final expression is the return value. A semicolon would discard the value and break the declared return type.

checks.prompt: Which word describes the value a function gives back? Type one word.
checks.explanation: The value a function hands back is its return value, and its type is declared after the arrow.

lessons.title: Who owns a value
lessons.summary: One owner per value, moves instead of copies, and why a String cannot be used after it is handed over.
objectives: State the ownership rule in one sentence.
Explain the difference between a move and a copy.
Predict which line of a program fails after a value is moved.

sections.heading: Every value has exactly one owner
sections.body: An owner is the binding responsible for a value. When the owner goes out of scope, the value is freed. Handing a value to another binding transfers that responsibility, which Rust calls a move.

sections.heading: A move
Move, copy and borrow
rows: let b = a; where a is a String
The value moves: a can no longer be used.
let b = a; where a is an i32
The value is copied: both bindings stay usable.
a is borrowed: a still owns the value and both can be read.

sections.body: A common mistake is assuming let greeting = name; copies the text. For types that own heap data, such as String, it moves it, so printing name afterwards does not compile.

checks.prompt: After let first = String::from("hi"); let second = first; what happened to first?
options: It was moved, so it can no longer be used
It was copied, so both bindings are usable
It became a reference to second
It was emptied but is still usable
checks.explanation: A String owns heap data, so assigning it to another binding moves ownership. Using first afterwards is a compile error.

checks.prompt: Assigning an i32 to another binding copies the value, so both bindings stay usable.
checks.explanation: Simple number types implement Copy, so the assignment duplicates the value instead of moving it.

checks.prompt: Which Rust rule says that every value has exactly one owner? Type one word.
checks.explanation: Ownership is the rule. It is what decides when a value is freed and when it can no longer be used.
